Subjects
        
            Element cyclesEnvironmental health

AbstractMarine oxygen deficient and dead zones are economically and ecologically important regions with unique impacts on marine nutrient cycling and biogeochemistry. Climatic impact-drivers expected to affect oxygen deficient zones and associated nutrient cycles include changes in temperature, wind speed, and atmospheric depositions. These climatic impact-drivers will increase sea surface temperatures that reduce oxygen solubility, increase stratification and respiration, as well as induce changes in circulation that intensify upwelling and regulate the production and emission of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. Deoxygenation will impact biogeochemical cycles of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Climatic changes are likely to decrease bioavailable nitrogen and enhance sedimentary phosphorus remobilization, altering water column nutrient stoichiometry. Expansion of oxygen deficient zones can also have negative socio-economic and ecological consequences. Future research should focus on experimental and mesocosm studies, examine the responses of microbial communities, improve biogeochemical and ocean circulation models, and build and expand monitoring programs.

IntroductionMarine oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) in the present-day ocean are characterized by net oxygen consumption. Marine ODZs develop when community microbial oxygen (O2) demand exceeds O2 supply from physical circulation and in situ biological production processes1,2,3. These oceanic regions with [O2] of less than 20 μmol kg−1 currently account for about 8% of the entire oceanic volume4. Oceanic regions with [O2] <5 μmol kg−1 represent about 0.1% of the total oceanic volume5. In this review, hypoxic conditions are defined as water masses characterized by [O2] <60 µmol kg−1, low oxic conditions by [O2] <10 µmol kg−1, and anoxic conditions by [O2] <1 µmol kg−1, which is close to the detection limit of typical SeaBird electrochemical sensors6. These biogeochemically distinct regions have been expanding and shoaling in the past few decades, with negative biological and economic impacts4,7. Long-term studies document an O2 decline of 0.066 µmol kg−1 yr−1 at 300 m depth, a typical core depth for open-ocean ODZs, between 50°S and 50°N over a 50-year period (1960–2010)8,9. More recent estimates point towards a global ocean O2 loss of 2% (0.072 µmol kg−1 y−1) over the past 50 years10,11,12, a process known as ‘ocean deoxygenation’. A major question arises as to the biogeochemical impacts of ocean deoxygenation and expanded marine ODZs.The ocean’s major ODZs in the Eastern Tropical South and North Pacific, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal are generally associated with old and poorly ventilated water masses overlain by high productivity surface waters1,13. Coastal ODZs often co-occur with upwelling zones. Examples of coastal upwelling zones include eastern boundary upwelling systems, such as those off the coasts of California, Chile, Peru, Namibia, and Mauritania/Senegal (Box 1). Coastal upwelling systems bring nutrient-rich waters to the surface, which enhance primary productivity in the euphotic zone as well as organic matter supply and O2 consumption in deeper waters3,14,15. ODZs may also develop seasonally in regions, such as the West Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska4. Other marginal (shelf) seas or (semi-) enclosed basins, such as the Gulf of Mexico, the Baltic Sea, the Black Sea, Saanich Inlet, and the Cariaco Basin, experience areas of seasonal or complete anoxia or even hydrogen sulfide (H2S) accumulation in the water column, also referred to as “dead zones”16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23,24 (Box 1).In ODZs and anoxic waters, electron donors other than O2 are used for both heterotrophic and autotrophic processes. Indeed, the extent of ODZs is often evaluated by the occurrence of anoxic processes, such as nitrogen loss by denitrification and anammox4. These processes only occur under low-O2 or anoxic conditions and convert dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) to dinitrogen gas (N2), which constitutes a quantitatively important loss of biologically available nitrogen from the ocean4,25. Sulfate can also be used as an oxidant for organic matter respiration, producing H2S; prolonged anoxic conditions have been linked to localized fish mass mortality events as a result of accumulation of highly toxic H2S gas26.While the study of ODZ distributions and their biogeochemistry has gained considerable attention from the scientific community in recent years, including the effects of recurring climate patterns (e.g., ENSO: El Niño–Southern Oscillation) as well as mesoscale and submesoscale processes27,28,29, less is known about how climate change will affect biogeochemical cycles in ODZs. Dissolved O2 in the ocean is projected to decrease with high confidence over the coming century due to climate change30. This trend is driven by a combination of several projected high-confidence climatic impact-drivers31, including an increase in marine heatwaves, a rise in mean ocean temperature, and changes in wind patterns. The effects of other high-confidence climatic impact drivers on ODZs, such as sea level rise and ocean acidification, are not considered in this review.Ocean deoxygenation can occur directly, due to reduced gas solubility as sea surface temperature (SST) increases, and indirectly, through changes in ocean density stratification and ocean circulation and mixing24,32. Ocean deoxygenation greatly alters microbial communities and biogeochemical cycles, which influence the production of greenhouse gases, such as methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), with corresponding feedback on climate33,34,35. Yet, many unknowns remain regarding how ODZs and their nutrient cycling will respond to ongoing and future climate change.In addition, anthropogenic stressors, such as excess nutrient input, are expected to interact with climate change effects, further impacting ODZs. The development of anoxic dead zones in coastal areas is linked to eutrophication caused by high anthropogenic nutrient loading, particularly of nitrogen and phosphorus. Examples include the Mississippi basin36, Chesapeake Bay37, and the Baltic Sea38. This review evaluates the effect of climatic impact drivers (e.g., ocean temperature increase, changes in wind patterns) on the chemical forms and distribution of macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon) in marine ODZs. Emerging evidence reveals complex, non-linear feedbacks between O2 loss, nutrient regeneration, and microbial community shifts, which can amplify deoxygenation and greenhouse gas production. We also summarize potential linkages between ODZ expansion and socio-economic consequences and identify key research gaps and future research priorities for better understanding the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycle dynamics in ODZs and underscore the critical need for integrated, high-resolution studies to better predict the coupled physical and biogeochemical responses of ODZs to ongoing climate change. This review is building upon the efforts of the joint Group of Experts on the Scientific Aspects of Marine Environmental Protection (GESAMP) Working Group 45 (WG45), focused on “Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Impacts on Ocean Contaminants”. Pacific OceanThe open ocean and eastern boundary upwelling systems of the Eastern Tropical North and South Pacific Ocean present the most extensive ODZs, which occur between 100 and 900 m depth, with anoxic conditions at 300 to 500 m depth. The open ocean ODZ is deeper, more nutrient-limited, and persistent, whereas the coastal ODZ is shallow, highly productive, and influenced by benthic processes. The ODZs in the eastern tropical Pacific form due to weak ventilation, long water residence times, and high productivity from the coastal upwelling of nutrient-rich waters4. The evolution and shape of the ODZ are thus controlled by the balance between organic matter respiration (from high primary productivity in overlying surface waters) and ventilation via transport of O2-rich surface waters to the interior. As a direct advective pathway for O2 to these ODZs is lacking, O2 supply in these ODZs mostly depends on turbulent mixing processes, such as eddies and tropical instability waves164.A decrease in O2 concentrations in shallow depths (i.e., surface to about 1000 m) was observed in the Eastern Tropical North Pacific over at least the last five decades165,166. However, future deoxygenation in the tropical Pacific Ocean ODZs is not well constrained as there is considerable disagreement among numerical models in the magnitude and even sign of the net change in O2 levels57,105,167,168,169. A recent modeling study indicates that low oxygenated waters (O2 ≤ 120 μmol kg−1) are expected to expand as a result of decreased subtropical ventilation, while the core of the O2 minimum zone (ODZ) (O2 ≤ 20 μmol kg−1) is anticipated to experience a slight contraction due to changes in circulation and biological processes170. In contrast to eastern boundary upwelling systems in the Pacific, O2 concentrations in the ODZ of the eastern Atlantic are generally more elevated (O2 minimum ~17 µmol kg−1 in the South Atlantic and >40 µmol kg-1 in the North Atlantic13) and only seasonally turn fully anoxic and sulfidic close to the coast171,172. Despite higher O2 concentrations in the Atlantic Ocean eastern boundary upwelling system, the first open ocean dead zones have been reported in association with mesoscale eddies in the tropical North Atlantic91. Low-O2 concentrations (<2 µmol kg-1) were observed just below the mixed layer in the euphotic zone of cyclonic and anticyclonic mode water eddies generated off the west coast of Africa and transported offshore. In the nBUS, seasonal variations in dissolved O2 concentrations are associated with offshore wind fields, which affect coastal upwelling and circulation patterns174. Upwelling of nutrient-rich deep waters in the nBUS stimulates photosynthesis in the surface ocean, severely lowering O2 concentrations in bottom waters following organic matter respiration of the fallen biomass and leading to natural nutrient enrichment174,175.Coastal wind-driven upwelling occurs year-round in the nBUS, with more intense upwelling cells at Cape Frio, Walvis Bay, and Lüderitz176. While short-term upwelling occurs during all seasons, it is most intense during austral winter, due to the annual migration of the South Atlantic anticyclone176,177,178. During austral summer, the water column becomes stratified, leading to anoxic bottom waters and sulfidic events in shallow coastal waters172. Bottom water O2 concentrations are particularly low during non-upwelling periods or during Benguela Niños, which occur on a decadal timescale179. The large and persistent ODZs result from a high O2 demand from respiration processes combined with weak physical ventilation due to restricted inflow from oxygenated Antarctic Intermediate and Persian-Gulf Waters in the northern Indian Ocean. Ventilation age for these water masses in the Arabian Sea is 30 years or longer181, and consequently, suboxic O2 levels are observed between 150 and 1000 m depth in the ODZ182,184,185,186,187,188,188. Long-term decline in dissolved O2 levels in the Arabian Sea ODZ was reported183. The deeper part of the Arabian Sea ODZ (below 400 m) intensifies northward across the basin, whereas the shallower part (above 400 m) is in the central/eastern basin. The deeper Arabian Sea ODZ results from a combination of high organic matter remineralization and weak ventilation of intermediate waters. The eastward shift of the shallower Arabian Sea ODZ originates from stronger advection of O2-rich waters and eddy mixing in the western part, combined with the horizontal transport of particulate matter from the more productive western boundary or eastern continental shelf into the central/eastern Arabian Sea. This transport further enhances remineralization and O2 depletion in the central/eastern Arabian Sea183,185,186,187,188,188. The deoxygenation trends in the Arabian Sea ODZ are currently uncertain. Several studies suggest an historical decline from the 1960s to 2010 in the northern Arabian Sea189. Yet, despite a large seasonal variability in primary productivity in surface waters of the Arabian Sea, modeling efforts suggest a relatively balanced O2 budget in the ODZ on an annual average. This weak annual O2 cycle was explained by O2 supply (e.g., by Ekman pumping, monsoon currents, and mesoscale structures, such as eddies) and biological demand compensating each other seasonally and annually190. The higher input of freshwater also plays a critical role in this region, resulting in enhanced stratification and a consequential reduction in nutrient availability to the euphotic zone. Some of these coastal ecosystems suffer from severe deoxygenation, often reported as dead zones. Coastal dead zones can be seasonal, like in the Gulf of Mexico or Saanich Inlet in the Pacific Northwest (Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada), but they can also be permanent, like in the Black or the Baltic Seas. Elevated nutrient loading, coupled with strong stratification induced by riverine freshwater inputs, promotes the proliferation of phytoplankton blooms. The subsequent breakdown of fallen organic matter leads to the deoxygenation of deeper waters. Additionally, higher inputs of organic matter due to coastal wetland losses, as well as physical stratification, intensify hypoxia in the Gulf of Mexico200. The spatial and temporal distribution of hypoxia is variable and to some extent related to the discharge volumes of the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers and their nutrient flux16. Saanich Inlet functions as a reverse estuary, characterized by the influx of freshwater mostly entering through its mouth. A shallow sill at the entrance of the fjord restricts deep water exchange and, together with high primary production in spring and summer, the bottom of the fjord becomes anoxic, and H2S accumulates below the sill depth201,202. For instance, ODZ regions with [O2] <5 μmol kg−1 remove 30–50% of fixed (or bioavailable) nitrogen from the ocean, while only representing 0.1% of total ocean volume40,41,42,43. The recent observed expansion of marine ODZs is expected to significantly affect biogeochemical fluxes and ecosystem dynamics. In Boxes 2–4, we review marine nutrient cycles under low-O2 or anoxic conditions and discuss nutrient dynamics in marine ODZs and dead zones.Box 2 Nitrogen cycling in ODZsNitrogen is a macronutrient required by all living organisms. Nitrate (NO3-), the most oxidized form of DIN, is the prevalent form of bioavailable nitrogen in most of the oxygenated oceans. The balance between bioavailable nitrogen sources and sinks controls global primary productivity and oceanic carbon dioxide sequestration. Whether the modern nitrogen inventory is balanced or not has been debated40,41, although most recent studies support a globally balanced budget on the time scale of ocean circulation42,208. The marine nitrogen cycle is strongly modulated by O2 conditions due to the sensitivity of several processes to O2. While negative, (stabilizing) feedbacks that counteract perturbations and maintain a degree of homeostasis in the global oceanic nitrogen inventory generally dominate on global scales, local or temporary positive feedbacks can occur. For example, elevated ocean temperatures and higher concentrations of atmospheric CO2 promote microbial N2 fixation at higher latitude regions, whereas the rise in fixed nitrogen and acidification enhances the production of N2O, which in turn accelerates warming and establishes a positive feedback loop209,210. A classic example of negative feedback is the observation that an increase in N2 fixation leads to a rise in primary production and the amount of organic matter undergoing decomposition. This process creates anaerobic conditions (ODZ expansion), which, when combined with a substantial supply of nitrogen, promote denitrification, thereby converting fixed nitrogen back into N2 gas210.Nitrogen fixation, the conversion of atmospheric N2 to organic nitrogen by diazotrophs, is the main source of exogenous nitrogen in open ocean environments, although atmospheric deposition, groundwater, and riverine inputs can be important at certain locations111,211. Though nitrogen fixation rate estimates are low in ODZs212, microbes with nifH genes that allow for this process are prevalent and diverse in the three main ODZs (i.e., in the Eastern Tropical North and South Pacific and the Arabian Sea213). In addition, high diazotrophic diversity, but low N2 fixation rates, were observed in the nBUS214.Nitrogen loss in ODZs occurs under low-O2 or anoxic conditions, both in the sediment and water column, and follows two main pathways: denitrification and anammox25,215,216,217,218,219,220. Denitrification is the stepwise conversion of NO3- to nitrite (NO2-), nitric oxide (NO), N2O, and dinitrogen (N2) gas, mostly by facultatively anaerobic heterotrophic bacteria. The different steps of denitrification are sensitive to O2 at nanomolar levels25. Anammox is a chemoautotrophic process converting ammonium (NH4+) and NO2- to N2 gas and can occur where O2 levels are higher (up to 10–20 µmol kg−1)25,221,222. The relative contributions of denitrification and anammox to overall nitrogen loss are affected by the C: N ratio of organic matter223, inputs of reduced nitrogen through vertically migrating zooplankton224,225, and NO2- oxidation226,227,228,229,230. Additionally, the availability of organic matter also controls the partitioning between complete denitrification and N recycling pathways231. For instance, despite low O2 levels ( < 1–2 µmol kg-1) in the Bay of Bengal ODZ, N2 production by denitrification or anammox is generally low or not detected, as NO2- oxidation successfully competes for NO2- as a substrate232, but a small nitrogen loss is consistently observed based on nutrient stoichiometry233. In the Gulf of Mexico, sedimentary denitrification is the main N loss pathway, removing up to 68% of the total N loads234, while in Saanich Inlet, nitrogen loss by denitrification takes place in the water column as well as in the sediments21,235. Water-column N loss in the Black and Baltic Seas, on the other hand, is driven by chemolithoautotrophic denitrification, with H2S as an electron donor236,237,238. Likewise, in coastal ODZs, sulfide-driven N loss can temporarily play a larger role and even impact offshore ODZs through physical transport239. The main sources of bioavailable (or fixed) nitrogen in the open ocean are N2 fixation and atmospheric deposition. Near the coasts, river input and groundwater discharge represent important sources as well. DIN and dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) are assimilated by phytoplankton in surface waters. Below the euphotic zone, exported particulate organic nitrogen (PON) is remineralized or buried in seafloor sediments. Nitrification, the conversion of NH4+ to NO2- and NO3-, occurs in oxygenated waters. N2O is a by-product of nitrification. At low O2 concentrations ( <10 µmol L-1) or in the absence of O2, DIN is removed by either denitrification or anammox. Anammox is the autotrophic conversion of NO2- and NH4+ to N2 gas. Denitrification is the heterotrophic or autotrophic (e.g., coupled to sulfide oxidation) conversion of NO3- to NO2-, NO, N2O, and N2 gases. NO3- is also converted to NH4+ during dissimilatory NO3- reduction to NH4+ (DNRA). These processes also occur in sediments (not shown in detail). Low-O2 or anoxic waters can be upwelled to the surface, bringing nutrients into surface waters and potentially releasing N2O, a potent greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting substance, to the atmosphere. Dotted arrows indicate the release of gases.Box 3 Phosphorus cycling in ODZsPhosphorus is mainly delivered to the ocean by rivers, with atmospheric inputs playing a role only in oligotrophic regions259. The primary removal pathway for phosphorus is burial in sediments. Most phosphorus reaches the sediment in the form of settling organic matter. While some of this organic matter will be buried, most will be microbially degraded, leading to the release of dissolved phosphate (PO43-) to porewaters. This PO43- can either escape from the sediment to the overlying water or be sequestered in more stable organic or inorganic forms260,261.The cycling and burial of phosphorus in sediments is highly redox-dependent. When O2 is present in bottom waters, aerobic microorganisms in the surface sediment can store PO43- as polyphosphates in their cells, which they can use as an energy source262. A subsequent transition to anoxic conditions can lead to hydrolysis of polyphosphates and release of dissolved PO43- to porewaters, as demonstrated for sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in Namibian shelf sediments263. Similarly, dissolved PO43- can bind to iron oxy(hydr-)oxides in oxic sediments, and this PO43- can be released upon reductive dissolution of the iron oxides under anoxic conditions. The resulting elevated concentrations of PO43- in anoxic sediments can lead to the formation of a range of calcium phosphate minerals, including authigenic carbonate fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite263,264. The so-called sink-switching from organic phosphorus, polyphosphate, and/or iron oxide-bound phosphorus to apatite leads to permanent removal of phosphorus from the oceanic water column264,265. Phosphorus sequestration in apatite can be particularly effective in ODZ sediments with high rates of organic matter input but low rates of overall sedimentation and may even result in the formation of phosphorites266. Sulfur-oxidizing bacteria and other microbes are thought to contribute to such phosphorite formation, especially following redox transitions (oxic to anoxic264).Yet, when compared to oxic environments, a much larger fraction of the PO43- in organic matter that reaches the sediment returns to the overlying water in ODZ settings, as demonstrated, for example, for the Peru ODZ267. Redox-driven enhanced release of PO43- is reflected in elevated ratios of sediment organic carbon/total phosphorus with decreasing bottom water and sediment O2268, and was observed in ODZs, such as the Arabian Sea269. Importantly, the benthic release of PO43- from ODZ sediments is expected to increase upon increased deoxygenation and may contribute to a positive feedback loop between nutrient availability and further deoxygenation through enhanced primary production270.The release of PO43- from sediments to ODZ waters also confounds estimates of marine nitrogen loss calculated from NO3- and PO43- concentrations, where elevated PO43- would be interpreted as enhanced nitrogen loss (i.e., N* = [NO3-] − 16 * [PO43-] + 2.9 μmol/kg)271. Increased anoxia and/or hypoxia are key factors in internal feedback mechanisms. Anoxia increases N loss in the water column but also triggers phosphorus release from the sediments. Phosphorus release fuels large N2-fixing cyanobacterial blooms, which again increase O2 consumption during their remineralization, further enhancing deoxygenation272. Enclosed coastal systems with long residence times and a strongly stratified water column, like the Baltic Sea, are especially prone to such a positive feedback loop, while seasonally stratified shelf systems, such as the Gulf of Mexico are less likely to suffer from such a vicious cycle.Phosphorus cycle in ODZs. Dissolved inorganic phosphorus (DIP) or dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) is mainly delivered to the ocean by rivers and via groundwater discharge and atmospheric deposition. DIP and DOP are assimilated by phytoplankton in surface waters. In both oxic and anoxic waters, particulate organic phosphorus (POP) is remineralized or buried in seafloor sediments. In oxic sediments, phosphorus is stored as polyphosphate (Poly-P), iron oxy(hydr-)oxides (Fe-P) or organic phosphorus (Org-P). Sediment phosphorus can be released again as DIP, especially under anoxic conditions. Autotrophic silicifiers, such as diatoms, rely on Si(OH)4 and form the base of food webs while contributing to the cycling of N, P, and C275,276, and atmospheric CO2 removal through the biological carbon pump277,278. While coastal zones receive nutrients (including Si(OH)4) from rivers and submarine groundwater discharge279, pelagic bSiO2 production is primarily fueled by upwelling of Si(OH)4 originating from deep-ocean remineralized bSiO2279. Therefore, the regeneration of Si(OH)4 from bSiO2 in sinking particles and sediments is essential for supporting silicifiers in marine ecosystems. In contrast to N and P cycling, Si is not redox sensitive, and hence its cycling is only indirectly affected by O2 conditions. The rate of bSiO2 dissolution for particles that reach the seafloor is dependent on the degree of Si(OH)4 undersaturation in the sediment porewater and the available reactive surface area of bSiO2285. Under low O2 conditions, there is some evidence that bSiO2 dissolution may increase, either through more efficient microbial activity282 or increased degradation of diatom frustules286. Some other ecosystems, such as the seasonally anoxic fjord Saanich Inlet, have decreased bSiO2 dissolution at the sediment-water interface in anoxic compared to oxygenated zones281. The primary source of Si(OH)4 to the oceanic water column is from upwelling of deep-ocean Si(OH)4, which originates from remineralization of biogenic silica (bSiO2). Coastal zones also receive contributions from river input and groundwater discharge. In surface waters, Si(OH)4 is assimilated by siliceous phytoplankton, mostly diatoms. Biogenic silica dissolution occurs in both oxic and anoxic waters and in sediments. The activity of benthic macrofauna indirectly affects dissolution rates by changing the exposure of bSiO2 to varying levels of Si(OH)4- undersaturated seawater and/or sediment. In contrast to the N and P cycles, the Si cycle is not redox sensitive.Impacts of climate change on ocean deoxygenation and biogeochemical cyclesGlobal warming greatly impacts the physical and biogeochemical processes that drive the development of long-term hypoxia and ODZs in marine environments, including metabolic rates, stratification, ocean circulation, and winds30. Changing winds impact upwelling intensity and atmospheric deposition30. Changes in precipitation and flooding alter anthropogenic nutrient inputs, which may amplify climatic impact-drivers44,45. In turn, ocean deoxygenation, amplified by changes in O2 solubility and associated changes in redox conditions, affects community structure and biogeochemical cycles39,46,47. The impacts of climatic drivers affecting O2 and nutrient cycles in ODZs are reviewed below. Hydrocarbon oxidation has also been associated with O2 and nutrient depletion, but it is not further discussed in this review (e.g., in the Gulf of Mexico45,48).Decrease in oxygen solubility and stratificationIncreases in mean sea surface temperatures (0.6 °C between 1980 and 2020)30 and marine heatwaves reduce the solubility of O2 and hence its availability to organisms49,50. O2 solubility decreases non-linearly with increasing temperature, e.g., corresponding to a decrease of 2.5 micromoles of O2 per half a degree Celsius (at 15 °C and salinity of 35)51,52. Therefore, the greatest impacts would be expected to occur in high-latitude regions that ventilate the ocean interior. The ocean surface temperature is projected to increase further between 2018 and 2100 on average by 0.86 [0.43–1.47, likely range] °C according to the SSP1-2.6 model projection and by 2.89 [2.01 to 4.07, likely range] °C in SSP5-8.530. Overall, warming is estimated to account for about 15% of global ocean O2 loss, and more than 50% of the oxygen loss in the upper 1000 m of the ocean10,12,24,53.Warming of the surface ocean also decreases its density, thereby enhancing stratification. Greater stratification due to warmer temperatures is primarily observed at low latitudes. By decreasing mixing and ventilation of the ocean interior, increased stratification promotes ocean deoxygenation10,53,54,55. There is a consequence of stratification that needs to be considered: a decrease in nutrient supply to surface waters from the deep-sea reservoir56. A reduced supply of limiting nutrients can lower surface ocean productivity and the subsequent export of organic matter, thereby decreasing O2 demand in underlying waters. If ventilation rates remain unchanged, lowering productivity would lead to higher regional O2 concentrations57,58,59.Changes in community structure and biological respiration ratesThe increase in temperature and decrease in O2 levels are expected to alter the composition of microbial and phytoplankton communities. For instance, different O2 regimes were shown to modulate phytoplankton diversity in the coastal tropical Southeast Pacific ODZ. New production was dominated by large phytoplankton (diatoms) with low N:P ratios ( < 16:1) in the ODZ. On the other hand, smaller (pico/nano and micro) phytoplankton with intermediate N:P ratios close to Redfield or higher ( > 20:1) were prevalent in more oxygenated subsurface waters above the shelf break and offshore. Interestingly, excess phosphate liberated from the sediments under anoxic conditions did not stimulate N2 fixation60.The biochemical response of the microbial community to variations in O2 levels is intricate and difficult to predict. This complexity arises because aerobic and anaerobic microbial processes can often occur simultaneously, even in waters with low or possibly negligible O2 concentrations. In recent years, cryptic cycling of O2 and sulfur in the anoxic zone has been discovered61,62. The expression of the metabolic pathways involved in nitrogen cycling, such as nitrification, anammox, denitrification, and inorganic carbon fixation, is also linked to changes in O2 and the distribution patterns of common ODZ microbes, such as nitrifiers (Thermoproteota, (formerly Thaumarchaeota), Nitrospina, Nitrospira), anammox bacteria (Planctomycetes), and chemoautotrophic denitrifiers (e.g., the SUP05 group within the Gammaproteobacteria)63,64. For example, Thermoproteota with active nitrification and inorganic carbon fixation are predominant in low-oxic waters, while the SUP05 group of NO3--reducing sulfur oxidizers linked to active denitrification, sulfur oxidation, and inorganic carbon fixation are more prevalent in anoxic waters63. The high abundance of SUP05 bacteria involved in inorganic carbon fixation under anoxic conditions indicates that this group is likely to play an increasingly important role in global ocean carbon and nutrient cycling as ODZs expand63.Warming also greatly increases microbial metabolic activity, respiration rates, and carbon demand65,66. O2 is consumed during organic matter degradation, with the highest O2 utilization rates in the upper thermocline59,67. Two main factors influence respiration: the supply of organic matter and the rate of enzymatic metabolic processes involved. The specific effect of temperature on biological respiration processes is influenced by several factors (depth, light, nitrogen, iron, and carbon limitation) that are overall still not well understood45. Increases in respiration rates due to warming will also affect other metabolic rates and associated biogeochemical cycling, such as nutrient limitation for phytoplankton68 or O2 production69,70. Warming and higher respiration enhance NO3- regeneration and recycling in the euphotic zone, which increases primary productivity71. Higher primary production above ODZs may lead to increased export production and O2 consumption below the euphotic zone due to the degradation and respiration of organic matter, potentially expanding these ODZs. However, metabolic activity in ODZs has been shown to decrease at lower O2 concentrations and under nutrient limitation in the Eastern Tropical South Pacific72. This decrease in metabolic activity may, in part, counteract the effect of temperature3,73,74.In addition to its impact on biological respiration rates, warming has been shown to enhance the cellular Fe-use efficiencies of N2-fixing organisms, particularly under Fe-limiting conditions75,76. Iron is an essential component of the nitrogenase enzyme, which converts atmospheric nitrogen into NH4+. An increase in primary productivity by N2-fixers at the surface could lead to increased organic matter respiration at depth, potentially contributing to the expansion of ODZs.Changes in ocean circulationChanges in ocean circulation could either increase or decrease ODZ ventilation45. For instance, the largest expansion of the equatorial Pacific ODZ was associated with a strong reduction of the equatorial Pacific circulation in Earth system models77,78.Fluctuations in near-shore hypoxia or O2 depletion in ODZs are also caused by changes in oxygen and nutrient concentrations of source waters. For instance, higher nutrient levels in source waters feeding the California Current coastal upwelling further increased primary productivity and resulted in enhanced export and respiration of the organic matter produced44,79. Both a decrease in O2 (−5%) and an increase in nutrients (+0.5%), which are realistic under current climate change projections, could expand the hypoxic zone by 20–32%. Interestingly, the combined influence from these biogeochemical drivers greatly exceeded the effects of strengthening in upwelling-favorable winds (10% increase) and global warming (3% increase) alone44.Oceanic mesoscale circulation, including eddies, plays an important role in mixing heat, carbon, and nutrients. Satellite altimetry records have shown that mesoscale eddies have been increasing by 2–5% per decade in oceanic eddy-rich regions due to ongoing climate change80. Mesoscale activity is particularly enhanced in eastern boundary upwelling systems81,82,83,84,85. Eddies may inject nutrients into the euphotic zone, enhancing primary productivity, particularly in the open ocean. In contrast, models show that eddies could suppress coastal primary productivity by transporting nutrients from the nearshore environment to the open ocean, and counteracting wind-driven upwelling in eastern boundary upwelling systems86. In the Eastern Tropical South Pacific off Peru, transport of highly productive waters offshore by an anticyclonic mode water eddy and subsequent high organic matter respiration rates promoted denitrification and near complete NO3- exhaustion (i.e., high N loss) at the center of the eddy27,85,87. N2 fixation and carbon fixation rates were concurrently enhanced in the mode water eddies88. Open-ocean low-O2 zones (with [O2] as low as 2 μmol kg−1) were also found to develop within cyclonic and anticyclonic mode-water eddies during transport from the northwestern Africa coast in the Eastern Tropical North Atlantic89,90,91. In this region, enhanced nutrient supply to the euphotic zone in anticyclonic mode-water eddies was shown to greatly increase primary productivity92. Denitrification and enhanced N loss were also reported within these eddies93. Given the broad distribution of low-O2 eddies, these processes could be relevant to all eastern boundary upwelling systems94.Similarly, changes in fine-scale ocean currents could increase periodic O2 intrusions into ODZs, sustaining aerobic NOB. These intrusions allow aerobic NOB to grow and consume O2 at the ODZ boundaries. In turn, anoxia enables anaerobic bacteria to replenish NO2-, creating a cycle that maintains the anoxic environment. Thus, NOB could provide major stabilizing feedback to ODZs volume under climate change and affect greenhouse gas production (e.g., N2O)95.Changes in upwelling intensityGlobal warming is expected to increase the temperature difference between land and sea and cause stronger upwelling-favorable alongshore winds in coastal regions, particularly at high latitudes, with both meridional and seasonal shifts in upwelling strenght96,97,98,99. Change in upwelling intensity driven by global warming is projected to increase nutrient supply to sunlit surface waters, and subsequently, export organic matter resulting from enhanced primary production at the surface and O2 consumption from respiration in deeper waters45. In the North Pacific ODZ, a study observed a concomitant increase in NO3-, PO43-, and Si(OH)4 and a decrease in O2 associated with increased wind-driven circulation100, likely related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation101. Other possible causes for these changes include mesoscale eddies, the phase of El Niño, and seasonal changes98. In the coastal southern Benguela upwelling system, despite a projected increase in upwelling intensity, no clear long-term trend in O2 concentration is observed102. The projected increase in upwelling intensity could reduce the extent of nutrient trapping by increasing the offshore transport of particulate materials. Reduced nutrient trapping efficiency could thus, in part, counteract ODZ expansion due to changes in upwelling intensity102.Upwelling intensity is also influenced by El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate phenomenon characterized by the periodic warming (El Niño) and cooling (La Niña) of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. This cyclic event influences global weather patterns, leading to shifts in precipitation, temperature, and atmospheric circulation. As such, marine heatwaves are heavily linked to El Niño, which is often responsible for extreme ocean warming. ENSO is expected to become more intense and frequent with global warming103,104. ENSO affects oceanic nutrient cycling through changes in sea surface temperatures, altering the distribution of phytoplankton and zooplankton in the equatorial Pacific. During El Niño events, warmer sea surface temperatures suppress the upwelling of nutrient-rich cold waters, reducing primary productivity, respiration, and apparent O2 utilization (AOU)59,105. Denitrification rates were also reduced (up to 70% lower) during an El Niño event, with strong implications for the nitrogen budget106. La Niña is characterized by cooler sea surface temperatures, enhancing upwelling, nutrient supply, and primary productivity. Elevated primary production by phytoplankton during La Niña events supports higher zooplankton populations, thereby cascading through the entire marine ecosystem. Water column denitrification is strongly amplified during La Niña events, driven by shoaling of the upper boundary of the ODZ107. Yet, the changes in solubility and apparent O2 utilization during El Niño and La Niña overall compensate each other, weakening the magnitude of O2 variability59.Changes in atmospheric depositionAlterations in wind patterns due to global warming will also affect atmospheric deposition of nutrients, particularly in oligotrophic open-ocean regions. Atmospheric depositions of NOx and dissolved NH4+ have tripled since the industrial108. For instance, the South China Sea is subjected to particularly high anthropogenic depositions due to its proximity to densely populated areas. An increase in nutrient inputs from the atmosphere was observed in this region and was associated with greater biological production, O2 depletion, and carbon export109,110. In contrast, ocean warming, acidification, increased stratification, and associated food web changes are also expected to affect reactive nitrogen emissions from the ocean. Elevated biological process rates under a warmer climate may increase the production of ammonia (NH3) or organic nitrogen that could efflux to the atmosphere111. The release of volatile nitrogen compounds into the atmosphere can decrease the inventory of fixed nitrogen if they are deposited on land rather than returned to the ocean, lowering primary and export production. This process may consequently reduce respiration and shrink the geographical extent and thickness of ODZs.Nutrients, particularly Fe, are mainly deposited as dust in subtropical waters of the Northern Hemisphere, which are closest to desert regions112. Atmospheric inputs of iron and fixed nitrogen could, however, be transported from their region of deposition in the subtropics to the tropics113. Atmospheric depositions were also shown to support new production in upwelling regions114. Another biogeochemical model suggests that atmospheric iron inputs could support more than 25% of the net oceanic export production, with smaller contributions from N (5%), Si (0.2%), and P (0.1%)115. For instance, iron atmospheric inputs could greatly increase N2 fixation (especially in N-limited regions)116 and primary production, enhancing organic matter respiration deeper in the water column and ODZs expansion. Yet, a global ocean model indicated that the influence of atmospheric depositions on marine primary productivity was minimal. Specifically, while atmospheric depositions contributed to an increase in primary productivity, this effect was offset by net nitrogen loss due to denitrification occurring in ODZs117.Increases in precipitation, flooding, and nutrient inputs in coastal dead zones and ODZsClimate change affects marine and terrestrial processes, such as precipitation and flooding, altering anthropogenic nutrient inputs into coastal waters from rivers and coastal groundwater118,119. Nutrient inputs, from anthropogenic or natural sources, either by rivers, estuaries, and their tributaries, or from coastal groundwater discharge, can supply nutrients to nearshore marine regions, which further exacerbate eutrophication and the potential for O2 depletion, intensifying low-O2 environments24,45,120. The effects of climate change on nutrient inputs and cycling from riverine and groundwater discharges in coastal waters are further reviewed in a companion manuscript120.Positive feedback on global warming from greenhouse gas production in ODZsAtmospheric warming is further enhanced due to the liberation of greenhouse gases, such as CH4 and N2O, that are naturally produced under low-O2 or anoxic conditions in ODZs and marine dead zones121,122,123. Thus, while nutrient inputs from atmospheric deposition, riverine inputs, and coastal groundwater discharge can enhance primary production and hence potentially act to increase carbon sinks, they can also stimulate the production of the potent greenhouse gas N2O, which is enhanced by low-O2 conditions124. N2O is 270 times more potent than CO2 on a per-molecule basis and is the main ozone-depleting substance in the stratosphere125,126. Coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs account for up to 35 % of total oceanic N2O emissions35,125,127,128, but it is uncertain how these fluxes might change in the future. The development of anoxic conditions in dead zones or in the cores of ODZs also favors the production of the greenhouse gas CH4, which predominantly occurs in shallow near-shore environments. CH4 is 27 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO2 on a per molecule basis125. However, while CH4 accumulates at relatively high levels in the anoxic cores of ODZs (20–105 nM)129, it is rapidly re-oxidized to CO2 in oxic waters. Consequently, total marine CH4 emissions (6–12 Tg yr−1) account only for up to ~6% of all natural emissions130. Production of these greenhouse gases, caused by lower O2 conditions in ODZs, further enhances warming, which positively impacts ocean deoxygenation (Fig. 1). However, a decrease in net primary productivity and export resulting from increased stratification, especially in low to mid latitudes, may lead to a reduction in the release of these greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, since they are emitted as a byproduct of remineralization131.Fig. 1: Effects of climatic impact-drivers on nutrient cycling (P, N, Si) in marine ODZs.Full size imageGlobal warming reduces gas solubility and increases stratification in the surface ocean (1, 2) but increases respiration and metabolic rates (including primary production rates and the amount of organic matter exported) (3), and impacts ocean circulation (4). Increase in alongshore winds impacts coastal upwelling intensity (5) and atmospheric deposition (6). Changes in precipitation impact the delivery of nutrients from rivers and groundwater discharge (7). Nutrient inputs from atmospheric depositions, riverine inputs, and coastal groundwater discharges stimulate the production of greenhouse gases and their emission to the atmosphere (8).The alternating phases of ENSO also drive large variability in N2O emissions106,107. Specifically, net N2O production is highly sensitive to oxygenation and changes in ODZ volume106,107. Thus, the response of N2O to climate variability might be even stronger than the response of denitrification, which could lead to larger production pulses during La Niña and minimum production during El Niño episodes106,107. Recent studies highlight that, under certain circumstances (i.e., high OM availability), NO3--denitrifying bacteria can extend N2O production into more oxygenated waters, making them a major contributor to N2O emissions in ODZs, an important finding for predicting future N2O emissions132,133.Another example is the northern Indian Ocean, where N2O production along ODZs and emissions to the atmosphere are spatially decoupled, with the majority of the N2O emitted in regions of coastal upwelling, winter convection, or turbulent mixing134. This finding highlights the important role of ocean circulation, which, along with environmental factors, controls ocean circulation that modulates N2O emissions135.N2O accumulation and emission from the ocean are sensitive to climate variability, but it is unclear if ongoing ODZs expansion will overall lead to increased fluxes of N2O and CH4 to the atmosphere. Further study is needed to examine these potential feedbacks.Socio-economic impactsProjected increases in ocean deoxygenation, the areal extent of ODZs, and changes in nutrient cycling are expected to have socio-economic impacts. Yet, the socio-economic consequences of climate change on ODZs, nutrient cycles, and marine life remain speculative due to the scarcity of statistically robust studies directly linking anthropogenic climate change to negative outcomes in ODZs and dead zones. Coastal areas provide essential ecosystem services, such as recreational activities, fisheries, transport, and energy production. The expansion of marine ODZs reduces the volume of oxic shallow waters where most human interaction with the ocean occurs and where many nutritionally and economically important species thrive. Certain microorganisms and marine animals that cannot carry out photosynthesis rely on aerobic metabolism. Minor fluctuations in O2 and nutrient levels can thus greatly affect marine ecosystems, along with associated services and functions136,137,138,139. Coastal regions, characterized by reduced ventilation and increased primary productivity, are particularly susceptible to deoxygenation. This vulnerability is exacerbated by multiple stressors, such as river influences, runoff, land use changes, and anthropogenic disturbances.Changes in O2 and nutrient levels within and surrounding ODZs and dead zones also impact fisheries and the livelihoods of human communities dependent on marine resources. Fish and shellfish industries will particularly be affected as fish are the most sensitive to hypoxia, followed by crustaceans, echinoderms, annelids, and mollusks6. However, it is important to emphasize that the taxonomic level of an organism typically provides restricted insights into the physiological effects of O2. For example, a study highlights species-specific variations instead of differences at higher taxonomic levels5. Organisms that are unable to move or possess restricted mobility, such as demersal fish, will be particularly impacted, along with benthic animals. Studies show that fish growth was impaired at O2 concentrations between 188 and 141 µmol kg−1 O2, while other aspects of aerobic metabolism are affected between 125 and 63 µmol kg−1 O26. However, even higher O2 thresholds have sublethal effects on animal behavior, ecological fitness, and geographic range, especially when the interactions with other climatic impact-drivers are considered (i.e., increase in temperature)5,139,140. Apart from supporting global food security, fish and shellfish provide many other ecosystem services, including supporting nutrient recycling in several marine habitats (e.g., coral reefs)141,142. The effects of global warming on fisheries systems also call for environmental and social justice considerations, as many impoverished and indigenous coastal communities depend on subsistence fishing. Climate impacts threaten their income, food security, and cultural heritage143,144,145.Research gaps and future research prioritiesClimate change is expected to accelerate ocean deoxygenation due to a continuous increase in temperature and impacts of other climatic-impact drivers, such as an intensification of alongshore winds and atmospheric depositions45. In turn, ODZ expansion could alter nutrient availability, thereby influencing global productivity, carbon sequestration, and greenhouse gas emissions. This review highlighted that physical and biogeochemical factors driving ocean deoxygenation and nutrient cycles are interlinked in complex ways, often synergistically, making it difficult to disentangle the impacts from individual climatic change drivers and nutrients. Also, the effects of warming and deoxygenation can be non-linear, leading to increases in metabolic rates as O2 concentrations decline to a threshold, beyond which metabolic rates decrease146. Future research priorities to better understand the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling in ODZs include improved 1) experimental and mesocosm studies, 2) microbial and genomic investigations, 3) biogeochemical modeling, and 4) high spatial and temporal resolution observations.First, more experimental and mesocosm studies are needed to isolate the effects of temperature, carbon dioxide, and deoxygenation on nutrient cycling in ODZs. For instance, it is unclear how ODZ expansion will affect nutrient regeneration versus loss by denitrification and/or anammox. The impacts of low O2 on nutrient stoichiometry (N:P:Fe ratios) and consequences for phytoplankton communities also need further investigation. Mesocosm experiments simulating future climate conditions in ODZ-like environments could help better understand the responses in nutrient cycling under isolated or multiple stressor conditions, such as warming, acidification, and deoxygenation. The feedback between ocean deoxygenation and atmospheric greenhouse gas fluxes (e.g., N2O) also requires further investigation.Second, a better understanding of the responses of microbial communities and marine organisms to warming, acidification, and deoxygenation is needed2. Several areas where more focused research is necessary include 1) investigating how the structure and function of microbial communities and higher trophic levels shift with changing O2 and nutrient regimes, 2) linking microbial diversity with nitrogen transformation pathways in ODZs using metagenomics and transcriptomics, and 3) studying how the antagonistic or symbiotic interactions (i.e., cooperation or competition) between microorganisms change under deoxygenation and warming.Third, current models often lack the resolution and complexity needed to simulate the interactions between climate-driven changes (e.g., temperature, stratification) and nutrient cycling in ODZs. A better representation of microbial metabolic diversity and its impact on nutrient (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, silicon) cycling needs to be incorporated into Earth system models147,148. The partitioning between denitrification, anammox, and nitrification under low-O2 conditions is also not well resolved, especially under in situ pressure conditions. Additionally, resolving future changes in atmospheric circulation, terrestrial runoff, and ocean circulation patterns and mesoscale features, such as eddies, will greatly improve biogeochemical models. Meso and sub-mesoscale processes, such as eddies, greatly influence ODZ biogeochemistry27,85,86,87,149,150. Socio-ecological models should also be used to evaluate the vulnerability of coastal communities to ODZ-induced changes in nutrient dynamics. This will allow the development of early warning systems and adaptation strategies for ecosystems dependent on coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs for fisheries.Fourth, the lack of high-resolution observations and long-term observational datasets is a major gap in understanding current and future impacts of climatic drivers on nutrient dynamics and fluxes in ODZs and detecting trends. Higher spatial and temporal resolution could be achieved by deploying autonomous sensors (e.g., floats, gliders, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs)) and establishing sustained time series stations in ODZs. For instance, interpretation of highly resolved O2 and nutrient data obtained from the Biogeochemical Argo (or BGC-Argo) program will help improve understanding of the causes of O2 depletion and associated changes in nutrient cycles in ODZ151,152,153. One recent advance is the capability to detect NO2- at high spatiotemporal resolution using BGC-Argo floats154,155. In the future, efforts should focus on developing ocean nutrient sensors, such as PO43-, that can be deployed on autonomous platforms. Satellite data could also be used to improve long-term and spatially resolved estimates of surface productivity and nutrient limitation in ODZs.In summary, future research should use interdisciplinary methods combining field observations, including both discrete and high-resolution datasets from sensors on autonomous platforms or satellites, laboratory experiments, and earth system modeling. Shifts in nutrient dynamics can alter fisheries, food security, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. Yet, many unknowns remain, for instance, the effect of ODZs or dead zones on Si cycling is still not well understood. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the drivers and patterns of deoxygenation and the effects of deoxygenation on biogeochemical processes will help better predict future ocean productivity, manage marine resources, and mitigate climate feedback.

items.title: MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030
items.description: MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine
items.body:
Sostenibilità

MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030

Redazione

-

25 Luglio 2026

Un tecnico in campo verifica irrigazione e colture, simbolo di filiera controllata e sostenibilità nel settore agroalimentare.

MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine, ha pubblicato nel 2026 il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 a Malagnino, in provincia di Cremona, per rendicontare i risultati ambientali, industriali e sociali raggiunti nell’ultimo anno e fissare nuovi obiettivi al 2030. Il documento, diffuso dall’azienda, registra la crescita delle materie prime da filiera controllata a 108.858 tonnellate (+26% sul 2024), la riduzione dei contratti in somministrazione del 68% e il rafforzamento del percorso interno certificato Great Place to Work.
MartinoRossi adotta il nuovo standard Vsme per il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025
La novità principale del Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 è l’adozione del nuovo standard volontario Vsme, Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard, ispirato ai principi degli Esrs e all’approccio della doppia materialità. Una scelta, spiega l’azienda, pensata per anticipare le evoluzioni normative europee e rendere più leggibili le informazioni rivolte a clienti, fornitori, comunità locali e altri stakeholder. Non un passaggio solo tecnico, dunque. Anche perché nel documento viene formalizzato il primo Piano di Sostenibilità 2026-2030, con obiettivi, target e indicatori su cambiamento climatico, risorse idriche, forza lavoro propria e condotta d’impresa.
“Il Bilancio di Sostenibilità rappresenta, anno dopo anno, non solo uno strumento di rendicontazione, ma anche l’espressione concreta del nostro modo di fare impresa”, ha detto Stefano Rossi, amministratore delegato di MartinoRossi. L’ad ha parlato di una gestione “responsabile, trasparente e orientata al lungo periodo”, aggiungendo che la sostenibilità per il gruppo “non rappresenta un semplice adempimento, ma un modello di gestione che orienta ogni decisione strategica”. Parole misurate, dentro una traiettoria già tracciata. E ora messa nero su bianco.
Agrifuture e Underdrip, la ricerca nei campi di Malagnino
Uno dei capitoli centrali riguarda Agrifuture, l’azienda agricola sperimentale avviata nel 2022 su 33 ettari di proprietà accanto allo stabilimento di Malagnino. È qui che agronomi e ricercatori lavorano, in collaborazione con università e clienti, su produzione agricola sostenibile, nuove varietà, ibridi più adatti ai processi aziendali, precision farming, biostimolanti e consociazione delle colture. Un laboratorio all’aperto, con parcelle osservate stagione dopo stagione. Non una vetrina, ma un campo di prova.Leggi ancheNuovo bonus in arrivo a maggio: ti spettano fino a 1200 euro, come fare domandaRompicapo geniale, se riesci ad aprire la cassaforte hai un’intelligenza superiore: sfida subito la tua mente
Tra i progetti testati in Agrifuture c’è Underdrip, tecnologia nata da un’idea del presidente Giorgio Rossi e sviluppata con l’Università degli Studi di Milano. Il sistema brevettato di subirrigazione di precisione distribuisce acqua e fertilizzanti sotto le radici, migliorando l’efficienza d’uso delle risorse e consentendo l’applicazione localizzata di biostimolanti. Secondo i dati riportati dall’azienda, rispetto ai metodi convenzionali le pratiche di agricoltura conservativa hanno evidenziato una riduzione del 50% delle emissioni di CO₂, un calo del 50-60% del consumo d’acqua e dell’inquinamento di aria e acqua, oltre a una riduzione del 90% della lisciviazione di nitrati in falda. Dal 2025, inoltre, le sperimentazioni su Underdrip sono state orientate anche all’efficienza nell’utilizzo dell’azoto, mentre l’ERSA, Ente Regionale per lo Sviluppo Agricolo, effettua campionamenti semestrali su qualità del suolo e biodiversità microbica.
Filiera controllata in crescita: oltre 108mila tonnellate di materie prime
Le pratiche sviluppate nei campi sperimentali ricadono poi sulla filiera agricola, che resta il centro del modello industriale di MartinoRossi. Nel 2025 le materie prime provenienti da filiera controllata sono salite a 108.858 tonnellate, contro le 86.466 tonnellate del 2024, con una crescita del 26%. In parallelo, gli approvvigionamenti esterni sono scesi del 18%, fermandosi a 23.542 tonnellate. È un dato che racconta una scelta precisa: più controllo diretto, meno dipendenza da canali esterni. E, di conseguenza, una tracciabilità più stretta.
A presidiare questo sistema è Campi d’Italia, business unit incaricata di coordinare oltre 700 partner agricoli su più di 16.000 ettari coltivati. L’obiettivo dichiarato è garantire materie prime di alta qualità, prive di allergeni e Ogm, attraverso controlli lungo l’intera catena del valore. Nel frattempo l’azienda ha proseguito il piano di sviluppo industriale avviato anche grazie al Pnrr, con interventi pensati per aumentare la capacità produttiva, migliorare l’efficienza dei processi e ridurre i consumi energetici. Una crescita, insomma, legata ai campi ma anche agli impianti.
Persone, occupazione e Piano 2030: più stabilità nel gruppo
Accanto a ricerca, filiera e investimenti, il bilancio dedica spazio alla dimensione interna dell’azienda. Nel 2025 l’organico di MartinoRossi è passato da 120 a 141 dipendenti, con un incremento del 17,5%, accompagnato dall’ingresso di nuove competenze e da un rafforzamento manageriale. La certificazione Great Place to Work, ottenuta con l’89% di partecipazione al sondaggio interno, ha registrato un punteggio finale superiore di 22 punti rispetto alla media nazionale. Un segnale, secondo l’azienda, del lavoro svolto su fiducia, rispetto e valorizzazione delle persone.
Il dato più concreto, però, riguarda la stabilizzazione: i contratti in somministrazione si sono ridotti del 68% rispetto al 2024. In una fase di espansione produttiva, non è un dettaglio secondario. Nella nota che accompagna il documento, MartinoRossi spiega che il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 e il nuovo Piano 2030 confermano l’impegno a integrare obiettivi ambientali, sociali e industriali nella strategia di crescita, con target misurabili per i prossimi anni. La rotta, almeno sulla carta, è tracciata: meno impatti, più filiera controllata, più stabilità per chi lavora nel gruppo.

Concluse le analisi integrative sui campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati attorno all’area dell’incendio: IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene sono presenti in concentrazioni molto basse e non costituiscono contaminazione ambientale. Trascurabile la presenza di metalli pesanti.

I risultati delle analisi concluse il 23 luglio 2026 integrano i dati di quelle concluse lo scorso 17 luglio e si riferiscono agli otto campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati il 13 luglio a seguito dell’incendio all’azienda Spedi a Vecchiano (Pisa).
Nello specifico, i prelievi sono stati effettuati in sette punti considerati di massima ricaduta delle polveri e in un punto di “bianco”, situato in un’area non interessata dalla ricaduta.
Esito dei rilievi e inquinanti analizzati (vedi Rapporti di prova):

Diossine, Furani e PCB: come già comunicato, in nessuno degli otto campioni si registra la presenza di contaminazione da Diossine, Furani o PCB;
IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene: le ultime analisi concluse indicano la presenza di IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene, ma in concentrazioni estremamente basse e tali da non prefigurare un fenomeno di contaminazione ambientale;
Metalli pesanti: in base alla tipologia di materiale bruciato segnalata dalle autorità competenti, si è scelta l’estensione delle indagini anche ai metalli pesanti. Da queste analisi non sono emerse concentrazioni significative, fatta eccezione per Ferro, Alluminio e, in misura minore, Manganese. Trattandosi di elementi ubiquitari (naturalmente presenti nell’ambiente), la loro presenza non è necessariamente riconducibile alla ricaduta delle polveri dell’incendio.

Prosegue ancora la ricerca degli inquinanti riportati sopra, in campioni di filtri del PM10 di alcune stazioni di monitoraggio, tra le quali quella di Pisa Passi.

items.title: Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia
items.description: A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono sta
items.body:
Ambiente

Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia

Redazione

-

24 Luglio 2026

Operatori specializzati ispezionano un laboratorio dismesso messo in sicurezza, con area transennata e presenza di soccorritori.

A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono stati trovati nei giorni scorsi circa cinque chilogrammi di acido picrico secco e cristallizzato, una sostanza instabile che ha imposto lo stop immediato del cantiere per evitare rischi a tecnici e residenti. Il materiale, secondo quanto riferito dal CoGePir, il Consorzio Gestione Pirotecnici, era conservato in condizioni tali da renderlo sensibile a urti, vibrazioni, attrito e variazioni di temperatura.
Ex Caffaro, cantiere fermato dopo il ritrovamento dell’acido picrico
La segnalazione è partita dall’azienda impegnata nella messa in sicurezza dell’ex Caffaro, area industriale da anni al centro di interventi ambientali complessi. Dopo l’esame delle immagini inviate dal cantiere, il direttore generale del CoGePir, Piervittorio Trebucchi, ha chiesto di sospendere le lavorazioni, allontanare il personale e avvisare subito Vigili del Fuoco e artificieri. “Non bisognava muovere nulla”, avrebbe spiegato ai tecnici, secondo la ricostruzione del Consorzio. Solo allora l’area è stata isolata.
La Prefettura di Brescia, in base alle prime valutazioni, avrebbe preso in considerazione anche l’evacuazione di una zona con un raggio di circa un chilometro e mezzo. L’intervento degli specialisti ha poi permesso di neutralizzare il materiale, rimuoverlo e trasferirlo in un luogo idoneo, dove l’acido picrico cristallizzato è stato distrutto in condizioni controllate. Nessuno è rimasto ferito. Ma il caso, chiuso senza conseguenze, ha riaperto un tema meno visibile: la presenza di vecchie sostanze chimiche dimenticate in laboratori, scuole, ospedali e magazzini di ricerca.
Che cos’è l’acido picrico e perché diventa pericoloso
L’acido picrico, nome chimico 2,4,6-trinitrofenolo, è stato usato per anni nei laboratori di istologia, nell’industria dei coloranti e, in passato, anche come antisettico. Il suo impiego si è ridotto proprio per i problemi legati alla stabilità della sostanza. Di norma viene conservato umidificato o in soluzione acquosa; il rischio cresce quando l’acqua evapora e si formano cristalli anidri, di colore giallo, capaci di reagire con violenza a urti, calore o sfregamenti.Leggi anche“In arrivo 40° C”, bomba sul meteo: il caldo africano non si arrestaIl caldo africano è alle porte, quali saranno le città più roventi di questa estate
C’è poi un secondo elemento, non meno insidioso: il contatto con i metalli. L’acido picrico può formare picrati metallici, composti più sensibili, soprattutto in presenza di vecchi tappi, utensili o contenitori non compatibili. Per questo un flacone datato, magari con tappo bloccato o cristalli visibili sul collo, non deve essere aperto né spostato. Sembra un normale recipiente da laboratorio. Eppure, in quel momento, anche una vibrazione può diventare un problema serio.
Cosa fare davanti a un contenitore sospetto
Le indicazioni diffuse dal CoGePir sono nette: davanti a un possibile contenitore di acido picrico secco non bisogna improvvisare. Il recipiente non va toccato, mosso, aperto o fotografato da vicino; occorre allontanare le persone, impedire l’accesso al locale e chiamare immediatamente i Vigili del Fuoco e le autorità competenti. “Il tentativo di svitare un tappo può bastare”, ha spiegato il Consorzio, richiamando la necessità di lasciare ogni valutazione a personale formato.
La gestione di questi ritrovamenti richiede un coordinamento tra pubblica sicurezza, Vigili del Fuoco, responsabili delle bonifiche e operatori specializzati nel trattamento di materiali esplodenti. L’acido picrico essiccato, pur avendo caratteristiche esplosive, non coincide sempre con un ordigno dotato di innesco. Proprio per questo servono procedure chiare: stabilire se mettere in sicurezza il contenitore, rimuoverlo o procedere alla neutralizzazione sul posto è una decisione tecnica, non amministrativa né affidata al buon senso del momento.
Vecchi depositi da controllare, smaltimento solo con ditte autorizzate
Il caso di Brescia non sarebbe isolato. Secondo il CoGePir, vecchi flaconi di acido picrico possono ancora trovarsi in laboratori universitari, istituti scolastici, strutture sanitarie e magazzini di enti di ricerca. Nel maggio 2026, riferisce il Consorzio, una scuola di Genova sarebbe stata evacuata dopo il ritrovamento di una piccola quantità della sostanza nel laboratorio scientifico. La prevenzione, però, non significa aprire armadi e scatoloni senza criterio: servono inventari aggiornati, verifiche affidate a personale qualificato e procedure di emergenza già condivise.
Quando l’acido picrico è ancora utilizzato, deve essere conservato in contenitori compatibili, senza parti metalliche, mantenuto umido e controllato con regolarità. Lo smaltimento non può avvenire negli scarichi, nei normali rifiuti di laboratorio o tramite trasporto autonomo: occorrono imprese autorizzate alla gestione di rifiuti pericolosi con caratteristiche esplosive, nel rispetto delle norme ambientali e di pubblica sicurezza. Secondo i dati forniti dal Consorzio, nel 2025 il CoGePir ha raccolto e gestito oltre 51 mila chilogrammi di rifiuti pirotecnici, mentre nei primi sei mesi del 2026 ne sarebbero già stati trattati più di 40 mila. Numeri che raccontano un problema concreto: un flacone dimenticato per anni, in fondo a un armadio, può trasformarsi in una minaccia per lavoratori, cittadini e ambiente.

Per la rubrica “Dialoghi con l’autore e l’autrice” abbiamo intervistato Chiara Mezzalama, autrice di Dopo la pioggia

Dopo la pioggia, il romanzo di Chiara Mezzalama, affronta temi urgenti come il cambiamento climatico, cercando di coinvolgere le lettrici e i lettori non solo attraverso i numeri e i dati ma anche le emozioni. Ne abbiamo parlato con l’autrice in una caldissima giornata d’inizio estate, che è diventata spunto naturale per riflettere sulla crisi climatica e sulle sue conseguenze.
 
Nel romanzo emerge chiaramente l’idea che dati e statistiche, da soli, non bastino più a raccontare la crisi climatica. Perché?
Negli ultimi anni è cresciuta la sensibilità verso questi temi, ma continuiamo ad agire con troppa lentezza. Per questo credo che sia necessario parlare anche alle emozioni. La crisi climatica è sistemica, riguarda tutti noi e ha conseguenze imprevedibili persino per la nostra stessa esistenza sul pianeta.
 
In questo senso, quale può essere il ruolo della narrativa?
Il romanzo può diventare uno strumento prezioso perché, attraverso i personaggi, il lettore vive esperienze che potrebbero essere le sue. Non incontra semplicemente dati o notizie, spesso catastrofiche, ma persone nelle quali riconoscersi. È questo il potere della narrativa: creare empatia attraverso le storie e rendere concreta una realtà che spesso percepiamo come lontana o astratta ma che invece è molto vicina. Se riusciamo a coinvolgere lettrici e lettori sul piano emotivo, diventa più facile sviluppare una consapevolezza profonda e, di conseguenza, spirito critico e volontà di agire.
 
Nel libro gli effetti del cambiamento climatico – la siccità, il caldo estremo, le piogge violente – non producono solo danni materiali ma incidono profondamente anche sulla dimensione psicologica dei protagonisti. Pensa che oggi ci sia sufficiente consapevolezza di questo aspetto?
Si comincia a parlarne di più. Oggi conosciamo fenomeni come l’ecoansia, ma anche la solastalgia, cioè quel senso di angoscia e di perdita provocato dal deterioramento dell’ambiente in cui viviamo. Pensiamo a un ghiacciaio che abbiamo visto da bambini e che oggi non esiste più: non perdiamo soltanto un paesaggio, perdiamo anche una parte della nostra memoria e della nostra identità.
Ci siamo però anche incastrati in un unico modello di sviluppo che sembra concepire soltanto la crescita economica, senza riuscire a immaginare alternative. Ed è proprio qui che gli artisti possono dare un contributo fondamentale. La loro libertà creativa permette di mostrare prospettive nuove e inattese. Molti stanno affrontando il tema della crisi climatica attraverso le arti figurative, il cinema e la narrativa. È un segnale importante, che può trasformarsi in una spinta all’azione e aiutarci anche a superare gli stati d’ansia che questa inevitabilmente genera.
 
Cosa possiamo fare concretamente? Il singolo può davvero fare la differenza?
Le scelte individuali sono importanti e possono contribuire a contrastare il cambiamento climatico. Dobbiamo però essere consapevoli che, da sole, hanno un impatto limitato se non diventano anche scelte collettive. La vera forza nasce quando cresce uno spirito critico condiviso, capace di diffondere una cultura ecologista. È così che prendono forma richieste sempre più forti nei confronti della politica e delle istituzioni.
 
Nel romanzo c’è una giovanissima donna che incarna proprio questo spirito ecologista. Che ruolo possono avere oggi i movimenti ambientalisti? E i giovani sono davvero più sensibili delle altre generazioni?
I movimenti ecologisti hanno un ruolo fondamentale nello sviluppo del pensiero critico. Purtroppo, però, la politica sembra ancora non ascoltare le richieste che arrivano dalla società e questo crea uno scollamento profondo. Nei giovani esiste una consapevolezza molto forte della crisi climatica ma la classe politica e spesso anche i media non riescono a raccogliere questa energia e trasformarla in cambiamento.
Esistono moltissime persone impegnate concretamente nel contrasto agli effetti del cambiamento climatico purtroppo queste esperienze vengono raccontate come episodi isolati, mentre in realtà sono sempre più numerose. La politica sembra trovarsi spesso in una sorta di zona cieca, incapace di tradurre in azioni concrete le istanze della società.
 
Lei vive a Parigi. Il modello della “città dei quindici minuti” può rappresentare un’alternativa concreta?
Credo di sì. Parigi è cambiata molto negli ultimi anni, soprattutto dopo la pandemia. Sono stati fatti importanti investimenti sulla mobilità sostenibile: limitando il traffico si è ridotto l’inquinamento atmosferico e quello acustico e molte aree urbane sono state restituite ai cittadini come luoghi di incontro e di socializzazione sia per bambini che per adulti. È un esempio di come le richieste della società possano tradursi in politiche capaci di cambiare realmente il volto di una città.
 
Vorrei concludere parlando della protagonista del romanzo, Elena. È una donna che attraversa una profonda crisi personale e ritrova la propria identità anche grazie al contatto con la natura. A me è sembrata una figura portatrice di speranza. È una lettura che condivide?
Credo che le donne abbiano una straordinaria capacità di ricucire gli strappi. La gioia è una scelta e, proprio per questo, contiene in sé qualcosa di rivoluzionario e di resistente. Il contatto con la natura è fonte di gioia, così come lo sono le relazioni con gli altri, che ricostruiscono il tessuto sociale.
Le nostre scelte dovrebbero nascere dalla gioia. È una scelta profondamente politica, che si accompagna all’idea del dono, cioè alla possibilità di liberarci dalla logica del tornaconto personale. Questo ci apre a una diversa idea di libertà, nel modo in cui viviamo il tempo e nelle relazioni con gli altri. Questo è già un modo concreto di cambiare il mondo che ci circonda.
Dobbiamo prendere spunto dalla natura, che ci insegna un’altra logica: non è efficiente, almeno non nel senso in cui intendiamo oggi l’efficienza. Basta pensare al tempo necessario perché un albero cresca. Per questo abbiamo bisogno di una narrazione diversa, capace di aiutarci ad abitare il tempo che stiamo vivendo senza lasciarci trascinare verso la rovina ma aprendoci alla possibilità di immaginare un futuro differente.
